cards.front: Recall a key point about Colour Theory and Mixing
cards.back: The colour wheel organises hues: primary (red, yellow, blue), secondary (orange, green, purple), tertiary (red-orange, blue-green etc).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Colour Theory and Mixing
cards.back: Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel and create maximum contrast and visual vibration when placed together.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Colour Theory and Mixing
cards.back: Colour has emotional and psychological impact — warm colours (reds, oranges) feel energetic; cool colours (blues, greens) feel calm.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Colour Theory and Mixing
cards.back: Tints (add white), shades (add black) and tones (add grey) expand your palette beyond pure hues.

cards.front: What should you know about fine art exam tips?
cards.back: Demonstrate understanding of colour relationships, not just colour mixing. Show experiments with different colour schemes. Annotate swatches with colour theory language. Explain WHY you chose a particular palette, not just HOW you mixed it.

Students often make mistakes with this topic. Wrong: A shade is when you add white to a colour. Correct: A TINT is hue + white (lighter); a SHADE is hue + black (darker); a TONE is hue + grey (muted/desaturated). These are three distinct colour modifications, not the same thing.
Select an artwork that uses colour expressively. Analyse the colour relationships and explain how the artist creates mood and meaning through colour. How has this informed your own colour choices?

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Colour Theory and Mixing
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Colour Theory and Mixing using appropriate art vocabulary. Identify techniques, materials and processes accurately.

cards.front: Understanding Colour Theory and Mixing in Context
cards.back: Colour Theory and Mixing is a fundamental aspect of GCSE Art and Design that connects to all four AQA assessment objectives. Understanding this topic requires both practical skill and contextual knowledge — you must apply techniques effectively AND explain how your work relates to other artists and designers. The AQA specification requires you to develop ideas (AO1), refine work through experiment

For colour theory and mixing, effective experimentation means testing multiple approaches systematically. Start by researching how professional artists approach colour theory and mixing, replicate their techniques as studies, then adapt and combine approaches to develop your own method.
